A set has elements but no structure about closeness; a topological space adds a topology that describes which points are near each other.

collocations: open set in a topological space

examples.everyday: My friend who teaches math said a topological space is just a set with a rule for which parts count as open.
examples.professional: Our team designed the algorithm to work on a topological space rather than a plain grid of coordinates.
examples.analytical: A topological space is defined as an ordered pair in which the topology satisfies the axioms for open sets, and every subsequent result depends on those axioms.

nuance.analogy: A topological space is like a map of neighborhoods without rulers: you know which places are next to each other, but you do not know how far apart they are.
nuance.etymology: Topological comes from topology, from Greek topos (place) and logos (study); space comes from Latin spatium.
common_mistakes: Saying 'topological spaces' as if it were an adjective plus a plural noun in ordinary speech when the phrase is a fixed term.
Confusing a topological space with a metric space and assuming distances are always defined.

senses.definition: Serving as, or relating to, a totem.

core.definition: Relating to a totem, an object, animal, or symbol that a group regards as sacred and as a sign of its identity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, TEM. The first syllable is a long oh, and the final -ic is a short ik, not a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in anthropology; in general writing it can suggest something symbolic and important.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use totemic mainly in anthropology, religious studies, and cultural criticism. In writing and speech it is also used figuratively for something that serves as a powerful symbol of a group or cause. It is not common in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Symbolic is a general word; totemic specifically suggests a sacred or identity-defining symbol that a group revers.
Iconic describes something famous and recognizable; totemic adds the sense of group identity and quasi-sacred importance.

examples.everyday: That old pickup truck is totemic for my family, because it's the one thing we all refuse to sell.
examples.professional: The brand's logo became totemic for the team, and any change to it triggered long internal debate.
examples.analytical: Lévi-Strauss showed how totemic systems organize social categories through the relations between animals and clans.

nuance.analogy: A totemic object is like a flag that a group carries: it means nothing to outsiders but defines the group to its members.
nuance.etymology: From totem, from Ojibwe odoodem, meaning his kinship group, passed into English through anthropological use.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as TOH-tem-ik instead of toh-TEM-ik.
Confusing totemic with totalitarian, which has a different meaning and stress pattern.

senses.definition: To land an aircraft or spacecraft.
senses.example: The plane will touch down in Heathrow at about 2 o'clock.

senses.definition: To score a touchdown.
To score a try.

core.definition: To land an aircraft or spacecraft on the ground or on a surface.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, DOWN, which carries the main stress. The "ou" is a diphthong, so do not shorten it to "dun."

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a standard, factual description of landing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this for aircraft, and news reports use it for spacecraft and sometimes for a plane that lands at an airport. In casual talk, people more often say "we landed" or "we're on the ground." It is also used in sports for scoring, so context matters. Pilots and air traffic controllers use it routinely.

distinctions.note: Land is the general and more common word; touch down is slightly more vivid and often used in news or announcements.
Crash land means landing in a violent or damaged way, while touch down is neutral and may be routine.

examples.everyday: Text me when we touch down, so I know you got in safely.
examples.professional: Operations confirmed the aircraft touched down at 14:20 without any issues.
examples.analytical: The mission's success depends on whether the lander can touch down precisely within the target zone.

nuance.analogy: Like a feather settling on a table, the plane gently makes contact with the ground.
nuance.etymology: From touch plus down, the sense of reaching the ground.
common_mistakes: Writing "touch down" as one word when it is a verb phrase; the noun is "touchdown."
Using it for a car or person reaching ground; it is mainly for aircraft or spacecraft.

conversation.text: We touched down in Denver right on time.
Text me when you touch down.
The plane touched down hard, and a few people clapped.

senses.definition: To mention briefly; to cursorily discuss.
senses.example: We touched on the subject of wages, but we didn't reach a conclusion.

senses.definition: To come or go to for a short time.

core.definition: To mention or discuss something briefly, without going into detail.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on "on," which is short and reduced in speech but still the stressed syllable here. In General American the vowel in "on" matches "cot," so pronounce it AHN, not AWN.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a brief reference rather than a deep discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in meetings, presentations, and writing to signal that a topic was mentioned but not explored. It is common in reports and speeches. In casual conversation, people more often say "bring up" or "mention." Saying you "touched on" something can also politely suggest you left out details.

distinctions.note: Mention is simpler and can be very brief; touch on implies a short but real treatment of a subject.
Cover suggests thorough coverage of a topic, while touch on suggests only partial or light coverage.

examples.everyday: My mom touched on her surgery during dinner, but she didn't want to talk about it much.
examples.professional: In the meeting, we touched on the vendor delay but postponed the full discussion.
examples.analytical: The author touches on the problem of evil in only a few pages before turning to other questions.

nuance.analogy: Like a skipping stone that touches the water briefly before moving on, the speaker touches a topic and keeps going.
nuance.etymology: From touch (to come into contact) plus on, meaning to come in contact with a subject.
common_mistakes: Saying "touch about" instead of "touch on."
Using it to mean "discuss at length," which is the opposite of its meaning.

conversation.text: The speaker touched on the topic of climate change.
We only touched on the budget in today's meeting.

senses.definition: Extremely sensitive or volatile; easily disturbed to the point of becoming unstable; requiring caution or tactfulness.
senses.example: It is an extremely touchy situation, with everybody's patience wearing thin.

senses.definition: Easily offended, oversensitive.
senses.example: He can be very touchy when you talk about his estranged son, so be as tactful as possible.

senses.definition: Inclined to engage in physical touch.
To touch.

core.definition: Easily offended or upset, or describing a subject that needs careful, tactful handling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TUCH, and end with a clear, light EE sound. The ch is a single sound, not two separate consonants.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing a person who is oversensitive; neutral when describing a sensitive situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for people who take offense easily, like "He's touchy about his weight," which can sound critical. For topics, "touchy subject" is a very common and neutral phrase. Calling someone touchy to their face can sound rude, so use it carefully in conversation.

distinctions.note: Sensitive is more polite and can describe feelings or topics neutrally; touchy often suggests someone is being prickly or defensive.
Delicate describes something fragile or requiring care; touchy usually describes people or topics that provoke quick reactions.

examples.everyday: Don't bring up his divorce; he gets touchy about it.
examples.professional: Salary is a touchy subject, so let's handle it with the HR team first.
examples.analytical: Debates about religious freedom are touchy because they involve both public order and private conscience.

nuance.analogy: Like a fuse that burns quickly, a touchy person or topic reacts at the slightest spark.
nuance.etymology: From touch, meaning easily affected by touch or feeling.
common_mistakes: Using touchy to mean physically affectionate, which is an older, uncommon sense.
Saying "touchy about" with the wrong preposition; use "touchy about" with a topic or feeling.

touchy.etymology: A variant of earlier *tetchy* (“cranky, easily annoyed, difficult to handle”), under influence from some senses of *touch* (“affect, disturb”) and simulating *touch* + *y*.

conversation.text: He's a little touchy about his weight, so don't bring it up.
Why are you so touchy today? I was just asking.
Money is a touchy subject in my family.

senses.definition: Any situation in which the quality or quantity of one thing must be decreased for another to be increased.
senses.example: In writing, there's often a trade-off between being concise and being complete.

core.definition: A situation in which gaining more of one good thing means accepting less of another, so you must choose between them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'TRADE'. The second part, 'off', is lighter and is often pronounced with the vowel of 'awf' in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a choice, so it is neither good nor bad by itself.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'trade-off' in meetings, planning, and everyday decisions. People say 'There's a trade-off here' or 'That's the trade-off'. A natural response is 'Okay, what do we gain and what do we lose?'

distinctions.note: A compromise means each side gives something up to reach agreement, while a trade-off means choosing to gain one thing by losing another.
A sacrifice implies giving up something valuable for a higher purpose, while a trade-off is more neutral and analytical.

examples.everyday: The cheaper apartment means a longer commute, so that's the trade-off we have to think about.
examples.professional: Lower latency is worth the trade-off in memory use, so let's go with the cache.
examples.analytical: The bias-variance trade-off is central to model selection, because simpler models generalize more reliably but can miss real structure.

nuance.analogy: A trade-off is like a seesaw: when one side goes up, the other must go down.
nuance.etymology: From the phrase 'trade off', meaning to exchange one thing for another.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong preposition, such as 'trade-off of' instead of 'trade-off between'.
Confusing 'trade-off' with 'compromise', which implies that both sides meet in the middle.
patterns: a trade-off between A and B

conversation.text: There's a trade-off between speed and accuracy.
What's the trade-off if we launch early?
Every option has trade-offs, so let's choose the one with the least risk.

senses.definition: One who teaches another (usually called a student, learner, or tutee) in a one-on-one or small-group interaction.
senses.example: He passed the difficult class with help from his tutor.

senses.definition: A card that allows one to search one's deck for one or more other cards.
To instruct or teach, especially an individual or small group.
senses.example: To help pay her tuition, the college student began to tutor high school students in calculus and physics.

senses.definition: To fetch a card from one's deck.

core.definition: A person who teaches one student or a small group, usually one-on-one and outside a regular class.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TOO. The final syllable is a reduced vowel with r coloring, so say it as ter, not tor.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. A tutor is seen as helpful and supportive, especially in school and college settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I need a tutor for math or my kid has a tutor all the time. Tutoring is common in schools and in private services. For a regular school teacher, people say teacher, not tutor. The verb is used in the same way: tutor someone in a subject.

distinctions.note: A teacher works with a whole class in a school. A tutor works with one or a few students, often outside school hours.
A mentor guides a person's career or growth over time. A tutor focuses on teaching a particular subject or skill.
A coach trains people in sports or performance. A tutor teaches academic or intellectual skills.

examples.everyday: My daughter has a math tutor on Tuesdays and Thursdays after school.
examples.professional: The training team will tutor new analysts in SQL during their first two weeks.
examples.analytical: Paul calls the law a tutor, a custodian who leads us toward Christ, rather than a permanent master.

nuance.analogy: A tutor is like a personal trainer for the mind: focused, close, and tailored to one person's weak spots.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tutor, guardian or protector, from tueri, to watch over.
common_mistakes: Using tutor for any teacher. In American English, a school teacher is a teacher, and a tutor is a private helper.
Saying tutor me in math without a preposition. Better: tutor me in math or help me with math.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word paidagogos (παιδαγωγός) refers to a household servant who guarded and guided a child, not a teacher in the modern sense. The RSV uses custodian in Galatians 3:24, where Paul says the law was our custodian until Christ came, and Galatians 3:25 says we are no longer under a custodian. The idea is of a strict guide for childhood, which is then ended by faith.

tutor.etymology: From Middle English *tutour*, from Old French *tuteur*, from Latin *tūtor* (“a watcher, protector, guardian”), from *tueor* (“protect”); see tuition.

senses.definition: Able to be forgiven; worthy of forgiveness.
senses.example: His venial youthful indiscretions.

senses.definition: Worthy of forgiveness because trifling (trivial).
senses.example: His venial youthful indiscretions.

senses.definition: Not causing spiritual death.

core.definition: Small enough to be forgiven; a minor fault or error that does not need to be taken as seriously as a serious wrong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'uhl,' not 'eel' or 'ee-AL.' Do not confuse it with 'venal' (VEE-nuhl), which means corruptible.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly forgiving: it calls a fault minor, though it still implies the fault is wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use venial mostly in religious, ethical or academic discussion, rarely in casual talk. In everyday speech, people say minor, small or no big deal. You might hear it in a sermon, a philosophy class or a discussion of ethics.

distinctions.note: Mortal describes a grave, serious offense that is judged severely; venial describes a lesser one that can be forgiven more easily.
Venal means willing to be bribed or corrupt; it is a different word, so do not use it to mean minor.

examples.everyday: Eating the last cookie was a venial thing, my mom said, but she still wanted an apology.
examples.professional: Missing one small deadline is a venial error, but missing three in a row will raise questions.
examples.analytical: Many medieval theologians argued that venial faults do not destroy the believer's relationship with God, though they still need forgiveness.

nuance.analogy: A venial fault is like a small scratch on a car: it needs attention, but the car still runs.
nuance.etymology: From Latin venialis, pardonable, from venia, pardon or forgiveness.
common_mistakes: Confusing venial with venal, which describes corruption or a willingness to take bribes.
Stressing the second syllable as in 'veh-NEE-al' instead of VEE-nee-uhl.

venial.etymology: From Old French *venial*, borrowed from Late Latin *venialis* (“pardonable”), from Latin *venia* (“forgiveness”).

senses.definition: Appearing to be true or real; probable; likely.
Faithful to its own rules; internally consistent.

core.definition: Seeming true or real, likely to be believed, especially in a story or fiction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'SIM', the third syllable. The final '-ar' is reduced to 'er' in American speech, so do not pronounce it as 'ar'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises a story or account for seeming real.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in literary criticism, reviews and academic writing. In everyday talk they would say 'realistic' or 'believable'. It can sound pretentious in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Realistic is common and general; verisimilar is more formal and specifically describes how convincing a story or representation seems.
Plausible means reasonable or likely; verisimilar specifically concerns the appearance of truth in fiction or representation.

examples.everyday: The movie's plot was a bit silly, but the characters felt verisimilar enough that I got caught up in them.
examples.professional: The training scenarios need to be verisimilar so that new employees respond the way they would in real emergencies.
examples.analytical: The novel's verisimilar details make its fantastic events feel plausible within the world it creates.

nuance.analogy: A verisimilar story is like a good wax figure: it looks so real that you almost forget it is not alive.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'verisimilis', from 'verus' (true) and 'similis' (like).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'verisimilitude', the noun.
Stressing the first syllable as 'VER-ih-sim-uh-ler'.
Using it to mean 'true' in a factual sense rather than 'seeming true'.

senses.definition: The state of being viscous.
A tendency to prolong interpersonal encounters.
A quantity expressing the magnitude of internal friction in a fluid, as measured by the force per unit area resisting uniform flow.

core.definition: A measure of how strongly a fluid resists flowing; the thickness or internal friction of a liquid, such as honey versus water.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -KAH-, and the first syllable is short, like 'vis' in 'visit'. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce the middle vowel as a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific or everyday descriptive term with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use viscosity mainly in science, engineering, cooking and automotive contexts, such as motor oil ratings. In casual talk people more often say the oil is thick or runny. The word is not usually used for people's personalities.

distinctions.note: Thickness describes how deep or dense something is in ordinary speech, while viscosity is the measured resistance of a fluid to flow.
Density is mass per unit volume, whereas viscosity concerns how easily a fluid flows; honey is both dense and viscous, but they are different properties.

examples.everyday: The mechanic said the oil's viscosity is too low for this weather, so we need a thicker grade.
examples.professional: We need to check the viscosity of the adhesive batch before it goes onto the production line.
examples.analytical: Viscosity expresses the resistance a fluid offers to shear, and this resistance is what distinguishes flow behavior in Newtonian and non-Newtonian materials.

nuance.analogy: Viscosity is like the stubbornness of a crowd: water slips through quickly, while molasses has to be pushed through slowly.
nuance.etymology: From Latin viscum, 'birdlime' or mistletoe sap, which was sticky.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as VIS-kos-ity instead of vis-KAH-sih-tee.
Confusing viscosity with density when describing how heavy a liquid feels.

viscosity.etymology: From Middle French *viscosité*, from Old French *viscosité*, from Medieval Latin *viscositas*; analysable as *viscous* + *-ity*.

senses.definition: The act of vituperating; severely blaming or censuring.
Criticism or invective that is sustained and overly harsh; abuse, severe blame or censure.

core.definition: Harsh, abusive criticism or blame; severe verbal attacks directed at someone.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'RAY', the syllable before '-shun'. Keep the middle vowels short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes sustained, harsh blame that is often excessive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use vituperation in formal essays, editorials, and literary discussion. Everyday speakers would say 'a torrent of insults' or 'a tirade' instead. It is a precise word, so it works best when you want to stress the abusive quality of the criticism.

distinctions.note: Criticism may be measured and fair, while vituperation is overheated and abusive.
A tirade is a long angry speech; vituperation is the abusive content of such speech.

examples.everyday: After the game, the fans poured out vituperation on the coach, and it was hard to watch.
examples.professional: The forum thread turned into vituperation within an hour, and nobody addressed the actual bug.
examples.analytical: The author's vituperation of his rivals weakens his case, because it substitutes contempt for evidence.

nuance.analogy: Vituperation is a storm of insults that keeps raining on the same target.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vituperatio, a blaming or censure, from vituperare.
common_mistakes: Using it for simple disagreement.
Confusing it with 'vituperative', the adjective.

senses.definition: Creating a synthetic copy of a specific person's voice.

core.definition: Creating a synthetic copy of a specific person's voice using AI, so the copy can say new words in that voice.

pronunciation.tip: Give 'voice' a light secondary stress and 'cloning' the main stress. The 'oy' in 'voice' is a clear diphthong, and the final 'ing' is a light nasal, not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical contexts; it can be negative when it refers to fraud or impersonation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use voice cloning in tech news, AI discussions, and security warnings, such as 'scammers used voice cloning to fake a family member's call'. It is not a casual expression and is most often used when describing the technology or its risks. Consent is a common concern in discussions.

distinctions.note: Voice synthesis creates speech from text, often with a generic voice; voice cloning copies one specific person's voice.
A deepfake is a broader term for synthetic media, including faked video; voice cloning refers to audio only.

examples.everyday: My mom got a call that sounded just like me, but it was voice cloning, and the scammer wanted money.
examples.professional: Our legal team wants a consent policy before we allow any voice cloning on the customer support platform.
examples.analytical: Voice cloning raises a question about identity: when a machine can speak in your voice, what remains uniquely yours?

nuance.analogy: Voice cloning is like a skilled impressionist who has studied one person so closely that the copy can say anything.
nuance.etymology: Voice comes from Latin vox; clone comes from Greek klōn, a twig, used for a copy from a single source.
common_mistakes: Saying 'voice copy' instead of voice cloning, which is the standard term.
Stressing 'voice' as the main stress; in this phrase, 'cloning' usually carries the strongest stress.

conversation.text: Voice cloning creates a synthetic voice that sounds like a specific person, sometimes from a short recording.
Scammers have used voice cloning to impersonate relatives asking for money.
We only offer voice cloning with the speaker's documented consent.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being watchful; alertness, vigilance or wakefulness.
senses.example: Continuous watchfulness is maintained around the clock.

core.definition: The state of paying close attention to possible danger or opportunity; alertness and vigilance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, WATCH. The -ful ending is reduced to a short uh sound, so do not say FULL clearly.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral: admired as prudence and care, but it can sound tense if someone seems constantly suspicious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in writing, sermons, and thoughtful or spiritual talk. In everyday speech they say be careful or keep an eye out. A natural reply to a compliment on your alertness is simply thanks.

distinctions.note: Vigilance suggests sustained, deliberate guarding against a known threat; watchfulness is broader and can be a quiet habit of attention.
Attentiveness means caring focus on a person or task; watchfulness stresses being alert for danger or change.

examples.everyday: The kids are at the pool, so we need a little watchfulness this afternoon.
examples.professional: Our on-call team needs constant watchfulness for alerts after the database migration.
examples.analytical: Scripture calls believers to a watchfulness that is inward as well as outward, a steady refusal to drift into spiritual sleep.

nuance.analogy: Like a lighthouse keeper who never stops scanning the dark water.
nuance.etymology: From watch plus -ful and -ness; watch comes from Old English wæccan, to be awake.
common_mistakes: Using watchfulness for one act of looking; it names a state or quality, so say a moment of watchfulness.
Stressing the -ful syllable instead of WATCH.
nuance.biblical_note: Greek grēgoreō (to stay awake, be watchful). Mark 13:33 RSV tells the disciples to take heed and watch, because they do not know when the time will come. Matthew 26:41 RSV urges watching and prayer so that one does not enter into temptation. 1 Peter 5:8 RSV tells believers to be sober and watchful against an adversary who prowls like a roaring lion; here watchfulness is spiritual alertness joined to prayer and discipline.

traditions.view: Watchfulness (nepsis) is a central ascetic discipline, a guarding of the heart and mind against harmful thoughts, cultivated especially within hesychast prayer.
Vigilance over the heart is taught through practices such as the examination of conscience, the Ignatian examen, and monastic custody of the heart.
Reformed and Puritan writers stress watching over one's own heart against sin and self-deception, while Lutheran writers stress alertness to God's Word and vigilance against false teaching.

senses.definition: Having the strength exhausted by toil or exertion; tired; fatigued.
senses.example: A weary traveler knocked at the door.

senses.definition: Having one's patience, relish, or contentment exhausted; tired; sick.
senses.example: soldiers weary of marching, or of confinement; I grew weary of studying and left the library.

senses.definition: Expressive of fatigue.
senses.example: He gave me a weary smile.

senses.definition: Causing weariness; tiresome.
To make or to become weary.

core.definition: Very tired from effort or strain, or fed up and no longer patient or interested in something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. Do not say it like 'wear' (WAIR); the vowel is short, as in 'WIHR-ee', and it rhymes with 'dreary'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests exhaustion or boredom, though it can be affectionate in phrases like 'weary traveler.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use weary mostly in writing, storytelling or formal speech, and 'tired' is the everyday word. 'Weary of' is common when someone has had enough of something, as in 'I'm weary of excuses.' It is not usually used for simple sleepiness.

distinctions.note: Tired is everyday and neutral; weary is more literary and often suggests deep or long-lasting exhaustion.
Wary means cautious or on guard; it sounds similar but has a completely different meaning.

examples.everyday: I'm weary of this rain, so I'm ready for some sun.
examples.professional: Our customers are weary of long onboarding forms, so we should simplify the first screen.
examples.analytical: Augustine describes the weary soul that finds rest only in God, a theme that runs through his Confessions.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who has kept going past the finish line of their strength, moving on sheer habit.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wērig, meaning tired or exhausted.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'weary' with 'wary' (cautious); the meanings are very different.
Using 'weary' for simple sleepiness in everyday talk; 'tired' is more natural.

weary.etymology: From Middle English *wery*, *weri*, from Old English *wēriġ* (“weary”), from **wōrīg*, **wōrag* (“weary”).

senses.definition: Of one’s own free will; freely and spontaneously.

core.definition: By your own choice, freely and without being forced or pushed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The final -ly is a short, unstressed ee sound, so say WIL-ing-lee. Do not add an extra syllable between the g and the l.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It emphasizes free choice and goodwill, often in contrast with forced action.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use willingly mostly in narratives and formal speech, such as 'She willingly agreed to testify.' In casual talk people often say 'gladly' or 'happily' instead. It usually appears before the verb or at the end of a clause. Use it to stress that nobody forced the person.

distinctions.note: Gladly emphasizes pleasure in doing something; willingly emphasizes that the choice was free and not coerced.
Voluntarily is more formal and legal in tone, often used for unpaid work or actions with no obligation.
Readily means quickly and without hesitation; willingly emphasizes choice and consent.

examples.everyday: My kids willingly helped carry the groceries in from the car.
examples.professional: Several team members willingly took on extra testing once the deadline moved up.
examples.analytical: The Gospel presents Christ as one who willingly lays down his life, not as a victim of mere circumstance.

nuance.analogy: Like walking through a door someone holds open for you: you go in because you choose to, not because you are pushed.
nuance.etymology: From willing, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'willingly' for 'willing' before a noun: say 'a willing volunteer', not 'a willingly volunteer'.
Pronouncing it as WILL-ing-ly with a long i in the last syllable.

willingly.etymology: From Middle English *willyngly*, *wyllyngly* (“intentionally, deliverately; freely, gladly”), from Old English *willendlīċe* (“diligently”), equivalent to *willing* + *-ly*.

senses.definition: To twist, wring (something).
To contort (a part of the body).
To twist bodily; to contort one's self; to be distorted.
To extort.
The number of negative crossings subtracted from the number of positive crossings in a knot.
(rare) A contortion.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To twist or squirm the body violently, usually because of pain, discomfort, or strong emotion.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a long i diphthong, as in ride. The final th is voiced, like the th in breathe, so it ends in a soft z-like sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes intense pain or distress, and it can be vivid or dramatic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use writhe in descriptions of injury, illness, or emotional torment, such as writhing in pain on the floor. In everyday talk people often say squirm, but writhe is stronger and more dramatic. It is also common in books, news reports, and movies.

distinctions.note: Squirm suggests wriggling from unease or embarrassment and is milder; writhe suggests more violent twisting, usually from pain.
Twist is a general motion; writhe specifically describes a body moving in agony or contortion.

examples.everyday: He was writhing on the couch with a stomach cramp, so we called the doctor.
examples.professional: The team member writhed in frustration as the deployment failed for the third time.
examples.analytical: The poem makes the speaker writhe under guilt, so the reader feels the tension in the body as well as the mind.

nuance.analogy: Writhing is like a rope being twisted hard in every direction at once.
nuance.etymology: From Old English writhan, meaning to twist, wind, or wrench.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like write.
Using writhe for mild discomfort; it is stronger than squirm.
Confusing it with rhythm or rhyme in pronunciation.

writhe.etymology: From Middle English *writhen*, from Old English *wrīþan*, from **wrīþan*, from Proto-Germanic **wrīþaną* (“to weave, twist, turn”), from Proto-Indo-European **wreyt-* (“to twist, writhe”).

senses.definition: The spirit of the age; the taste, outlook, and spirit characteristic of a period.

core.definition: The general mood, values and intellectual spirit that characterize a particular period of time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ZITE. The second syllable also has a weaker stress, and the final 'st' should be crisp, not extra vowel sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in essays, reviews, cultural criticism and formal conversation about history or the arts. It sounds somewhat literary, so in casual speech people often say the mood of the times or what people were into back then. A natural reply is to agree or add a specific example.

distinctions.note: Zeitgeist is a cultural idea about an era, while zeitgeber is a biological cue that resets the body clock.

examples.everyday: That movie really captured the zeitgeist of the early 2000s, with all the flip phones and boy bands.
examples.professional: Our marketing team wants the campaign to tap into the current zeitgeist around remote work.
examples.analytical: Hegel's notion of a historical spirit was later popularized as the zeitgeist, a way of describing shared assumptions in an age.

nuance.analogy: Like the weather of a whole era, felt by everyone even if no one can point to it.
nuance.etymology: From German Zeit, 'time', and Geist, 'spirit'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'zeit-GEIST' with a German vowel.
Using it for a single person's opinion rather than the broad spirit of a period.

core.definition: A minor Hebrew prophet of the 7th century BC, son of Cushi, who warned Judah of the coming day of the LORD and called for repentance.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NY, the third syllable from the start in the usual American pronunciation. The ending is a reduced uh, not a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a biblical figure and is used in religious or academic contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mention Zephaniah mainly in Bible study, sermons, or discussions of the Old Testament prophets. In casual conversation a person might say the prophet Zephaniah or the book of Zephaniah. The name is not commonly used as a personal first name outside religious families.

distinctions.note: Habakkuk is another minor prophet placed nearby in the Bible, so learners sometimes confuse their books, but Habakkuk questions God about injustice.
Zechariah is a different prophet of the post-exilic period, so the names sound alike but refer to different books.

examples.everyday: Our small group is reading Zephaniah this week, so we should check the first chapter before Thursday.
examples.professional: In my sermon series on the minor prophets, I am starting with Zephaniah because its theme of the day of the LORD fits our topic.
examples.analytical: Zephaniah's oracles against the nations and his promise of a remnant reveal a complex theology of judgment and restoration.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Tsephanyah, meaning the LORD has hidden or protected.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in ZEF-uh-nye-uh.
Confusing Zephaniah with Zechariah, which is a different prophet and book.
nuance.biblical_note: Zephaniah is a prophet who warns Judah during the reign of King Josiah, probably around 640 to 630 BC. Scripture identifies him as the son of Cushi, and his prophecy centers on the day of the LORD as a time of judgment that also leads to hope for a faithful remnant. Zephaniah 1:14 announces that the great day of the LORD is near. Zephaniah 2:3 calls the humble of the land to seek the LORD and righteousness. Zephaniah 3:17 speaks of the LORD rejoicing over his people with love.
